title: The lion inside
hookLine: Rumi ends: the outer enemy is gone, the lion within remains, the greater struggle (Masnavi 1.1373ff)
carry: a dragon that could drink the seas

lines: YOU FINALLY DEAL WITH THE THING.
IT PACKED ITS BAGS AND CAME ALONG.
cards: You finally deal with the thing. You quit the job with the awful boss. You move out from the terrible roommate.
You block the person who kept upsetting you. For a week, it's wonderful. Then you notice the anger is still there.
The worry is still there. The old habit is right where you left it. The problem packed its bags and came along.
The animals are dancing in the valley. The lion is gone. And Rumi, instead of ending the story, turns and speaks straight to his listeners.

teach.b: In plain words, Rumi says: we've killed the enemy outside, but inside there's an enemy worse than him. The clever hare can't trick this one into a well; wit and reason alone won't defeat it. Rumi's word for it is nafs.

In Arabic and Persian it means the self or the soul, and in Sufi teaching it often means the grasping, demanding part of the self: the appetite that's never full, the pride that has to win, the anger that roars first.
Rumi calls it a dragon that could drink the seas and still burn.
Then he cites a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, spoken on coming home from a battle: we have returned from the lesser struggle to the greater struggle.
The word there is jihad, which means striving or struggle, and the greater one, in this saying, is the struggle with your own self.

teach.h: A LOVED SAYING, A WEAK CHAIN.
teach.b: A note on the source: the saying is loved among Sufis, but hadith scholars have judged its chain of transmission weak, and it isn't in the major collections. Rumi uses it.
Some treasure its meaning; others question its source. Now put the story together: a lion, a clever hare, a well, a reflection. The outer lion was never really the danger.
The one to watch is the one you carry everywhere, the one who would have leaped at the reflection too. That, for Rumi, is the greater struggle.

how: In Sufi teaching, the struggle with the nafs, the grasping self, is described as the greater jihad, and the end of Rumi's lion and hare story is read by Sufi teachers as a statement of it.

o: the grasping, demanding part of the self
a holy breath given only to prophets
an outside enemy who leads you astray

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.

s: Rumi ends the story with the animals dancing
he turns to his listeners: the outer enemy is gone, but a worse one remains within.
in the saying Rumi uses, the greater struggle is with one's own self.
the lesser and greater struggle saying is in the major hadith collections
it's well-known and loved among Sufis, but hadith scholars have judged its chain weak.

games.q: the lion is gone and the valley is celebrating. what does Rumi say comes next?
o: the hare becomes the new king.
games.why: the outer enemy is gone, but the inner lion, the nafs, remains. wit alone can't trick it into a well.

practice: Ask quietly: what in me roars first? Anger, maybe, or wanting more, or needing to be right, or fear dressed up as control.
Don't fight it now; just see it and name it, the way you would name an animal you're going to learn to live with, then breathe low into your belly and notice what changes when you're still.

wordCard.voice: Nafs. The grasping, demanding self that Sufi teaching says is harder to defeat than any outer enemy. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic and Persian: self, soul; in Sufi teaching, often the grasping, lower self.

carryVoice: Your line: a dragon that could drink the seas. The greater struggle is the one inside. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: The saying of the lesser and greater jihad
sources.work: Hadith as cited in Sufi literature (e.g. al-Bayhaqi, Kitab al-Zuhd); graded weak by many
